strengths: The paper addresses a novel and challenging task: reconstructing sharp, animatable 3D human Gaussian avatars directly from motion-blurred multi-view videos, which has not been tackled in prior work.

The proposed 3D-aware physics-oriented blur formation model is well motivated. It integrates over sub-frame virtual sharp renderings obtained by warping canonical 3D Gaussians with SMPL-based motion, and uses B-spline pose interpolation plus a non-rigid pose displacement network to resolve motion ambiguity.
The authors provide both a synthetic benchmark derived from ZJU-MoCap and a real hybrid-exposure multi-camera dataset, which can support future research and benchmarking in this direction.

Quantitative results on both synthetic and real datasets show substantial improvements over direct GauHuman training and two-stage 2D deblurring + GauHuman baselines (e.g., synthetic PSNR 25.546 vs 23.081; real PSNR 27.010 vs 25.602).

Ablation studies validate several design choices, including pose interpolation, non-rigid pose displacement, LBS weight optimization, shape optimization, inter-frame regularization, control knot number, and number of virtual sharp images.
The paper acknowledges limitations such as foreground/background blending under sub-frame motion and dependence on precomputed masks, and points to future work.
weaknesses: The comparison is limited to 2D deblurring methods followed by GauHuman and direct GauHuman training; there is no quantitative comparison with recent 3D deblurring approaches (e.g., BAD-Gaussians, Deblur-NeRF) adapted to this setting, so the advantage over 3D-aware alternatives is not fully established.

There are notational/technical inconsistencies: T is used both as the number of virtual sharp images and as total exposure time; Eq. (10) uses t/T with discrete t = 0..T-1, which does not cover the full normalized exposure and may bias interpolation at endpoints. The notation {β_t, B_t} in Section 4.1 also conflicts with the later static shape and LBS optimization.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: no actual code or dataset link is provided, learning rates for different parameter groups are omitted, the weight for L_reg in Eq. (17) is not specified, and training time, memory, and convergence behavior are not reported.
The method depends on precomputed human masks and on SMPL initialization obtained from blurry videos via EasyMoCap; the sensitivity of the approach to initialization and mask errors is not analyzed.

Evaluation focuses on image-space novel view synthesis metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) rather than 3D geometry accuracy or motion plausibility, which may not fully reflect avatar sharpness, temporal consistency, or animation quality.

Some ablations show only marginal gains for individual components (e.g., shape optimization on the synthetic dataset), and the paper does not evaluate robustness to camera configuration, number of input views, or noise in camera calibration.
The title's 'Bundle Adjusted' framing is somewhat misleading because camera poses are not optimized; the method mainly optimizes sub-frame motion and avatar parameters.

strengths: The paper addresses a novel and practical problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable 3D human Gaussian avatars from motion-blurred multi-view videos, an important setting that is underexplored compared to static-scene deblurring.

The proposed 3D-aware blur formation model is physically grounded and integrates naturally with an SMPL-based sub-frame motion model, enabling joint optimization of avatar parameters and motion from blurry observations.

The construction of both a synthetic benchmark derived from ZJU-MoCap and a real 360-degree hybrid-exposure dataset is a significant contribution; the released data and code will support future work in this area.

Experiments are extensive: comparisons against several 2D deblurring plus 3DGS avatar baselines, ablations on key components, robustness tests under different blur magnitudes, and analyses of control-knot and virtual-image hyperparameters.
The method achieves consistent quantitative gains on both synthetic and real datasets, and qualitative results show fewer artifacts than two-stage deblurring-plus-avatar baselines.
weaknesses: The baseline suite is limited to 2D deblurring methods combined with GauHuman; there is no comparison with recent 3D/4D deblurring or bundle-adjusted methods (e.g., BAD-NeRF, BAD-Gaussians, DyBluRF) adapted to dynamic human avatars, so the claim of surpassing existing baselines is narrower than stated.

The title's 'Bundle Adjusted' is not clearly justified: the method does not appear to jointly optimize camera extrinsics/intrinsics, instead relying on pre-calibrated static cameras and precomputed SMPL/segmentation masks. Camera calibration details for the real dataset are not provided in the main paper.

Several proposed components yield only marginal improvements in ablations, e.g., LBS optimization and shape optimization give <0.1 dB gains on the synthetic dataset, weakening the case for their necessity.

Reproducibility is partially limited: the architectures of the non-rigid displacement network and LBS-delta network, training hyperparameters, and the exact real-data calibration/segmentation pipeline are not fully specified in the main paper.

Quantitative evaluation crops images to human bounding boxes, ignoring background reconstruction and blending effects; since blur also affects the background and the authors acknowledge background blending as a limitation, full-scene metrics would be more informative.
The real dataset covers only a limited number of scenes and subjects; generalization to diverse human motions, clothing, and lighting conditions is not established.
There are presentation issues, including a duplicated related-work paragraph and some notation conflicts, e.g., calligraphic R for rasterization versus bold R for camera extrinsics.

strengths: Addresses a novel and practically relevant problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable 3D human Gaussian avatars directly from motion-blurred multi-view videos, rather than treating deblurring as a separate 2D preprocessing step.

Contributes useful benchmarking resources: a synthetic dataset derived from ZJU-MoCap and a real 360-degree hybrid-exposure capture system with synchronized blurry and sharp cameras (Fig. 3, Table 1).

Proposes a coherent 3D-aware blur formation model that averages sub-frame renderings and couples it with SMPL-based sub-frame motion, B-spline pose interpolation, and non-rigid pose displacement (Eqs. 7-14).
Ablation studies systematically validate the roles of pose interpolation, non-rigid displacement, LBS optimization, shape optimization, and inter-frame regularization (Tables 4-9).
Reports consistent quantitative improvements over direct and two-stage 2D deblurring + GauHuman baselines on both synthetic and real datasets (Tables 2-3, 8-9).
Discusses an honest limitation regarding foreground-background blending under motion blur (Fig. 8).
weaknesses: Technical novelty is incremental: averaging rendered sub-frame images to model blur is standard in NeRF/3DGS deblurring (e.g., Deblur-NeRF, BAD-NeRF, BAD-Gaussians). Extending this to SMPL-based human avatars is a straightforward application, and the paper does not compare against any 3D-aware deblurring method adapted to dynamic human scenes.

The LBS weight optimization is technically ill-defined. SMPL LBS weights are defined per SMPL vertex, but the paper states that a deformation estimation network processes the coordinates of all 3D Gaussians to predict an offset δ. It is unclear how densified/pruned Gaussians are assigned LBS weights, how dimensions match, or whether the body prior is preserved. This undermines both technical soundness and reproducibility.

Key implementation details are missing: architectures for G_disp and the LBS offset network, number of Gaussians, initialization strategy, training schedule, runtime, memory usage, and code/dataset URLs are not provided. Reproducibility is therefore poor for a CVPR submission.

Baselines are limited. The strongest comparisons are 2D deblurring methods (RVRT, VRT, BSST, ShiftNet) followed by GauHuman, but no comparison is made to recent 3D deblurring methods (e.g., BAD-Gaussians, DP-NeRF, Deblur-NeRF) adapted to the dynamic setting, nor to an upper bound trained on sharp frames. The claim of surpassing existing baselines is therefore overstated.

The synthetic blur generation relies on RIFE interpolation followed by frame averaging, which may not faithfully model physical motion blur. The real dataset is small (8 scenes, only 4 blurry training views), and the real-data improvement over the best baseline is modest (~1.4 dB PSNR), with no statistical significance analysis.

The real-data pipeline uses EasyMoCap and Segment-Anything on blurry frames for SMPL initialization and masks; errors from these blurry inputs can propagate into the avatar reconstruction, and this is not analyzed.

Writing and notation issues: Section 2.1 contains a duplicated paragraph; pose parameter notation (Θ, Θ_hat, Θ_tilde) is inconsistent; the B-spline interpolation matrix is poorly explained; and the inter-frame regularization applies an L2 loss directly to rotation parameters, which is not an appropriate distance for rotations.

Evaluation is limited to per-frame image metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) on held-out views; there is no quantitative evaluation of animation quality (novel poses), temporal consistency, or dynamic fidelity, which are central claims of an 'animatable' avatar method.

strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable 3D human Gaussian avatars directly from blurry multi-view videos, with a clear real-world motivation and a stated benchmark contribution.

Proposes a coherent 3D-aware blur formation model that integrates virtual sharp renders over the exposure period under SMPL-driven motion, enabling joint optimization of the canonical 3DGS avatar and sub-frame motion parameters.

Includes a well-motivated motion model with B-spline sequential pose interpolation, a pose-deformation CNN, and inter-frame geodesic regularization to resolve motion-direction ambiguities in blur interpretation.

Provides substantial empirical support: on synthetic data, Ours achieves 25.55 PSNR vs 23.08 for GauHuman and 23.08 for BSST+GauHuman; on real data, 27.01 PSNR vs 25.60 for GauHuman, with consistent SSIM/LPIPS gains.

Ablations are extensive and mostly convincing, covering interpolation vs. independent poses, pose deformation, LBS optimization, shape optimization, inter-frame regularization, trajectory representation, control-knot number, virtual-frame number, blur magnitude, view count, and mask quality.
Qualitative results, novel-pose animation on AMASS, and an iPhone demo help demonstrate generality; code and datasets are promised for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: averaging rendered sharp images over exposure is a standard blur-formation strategy in deblurring NeRF/3DGS work, and the main extension is coupling it with an SMPL-based avatar model. A direct comparison to 3D-aware deblurring baselines (e.g., BARD-GS or Deblur-NeRF adapted to avatars) is missing, so the advantage of 3D-aware blur modeling over strong 3D deblurring baselines is not fully isolated.

The real-world evaluation uses only 8 scenes from a specific hybrid-exposure capture system, and the synthetic benchmark uses 6 subjects with blur synthesized by averaging sRGB sharp frames. The latter may not reflect physical linear-space blur formation, a limitation the authors acknowledge but do not quantitatively address.

The LBS weight offset delta predicted by a CNN from 3D Gaussian coordinates is described only briefly. It is unclear how these offsets relate to SMPL skinning weights and whether the improvement comes from principled motion modeling or from extra network capacity.

The method depends on off-the-shelf SMPL initialization (EasyMocap) and masks (SAM). Although robustness to perturbation is shown, failure cases under severe pose-estimation error or missing/incorrect masks are not thoroughly analyzed.
Evaluation focuses on image-space metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) and does not quantitatively assess motion estimation accuracy or animation quality, despite the motion model being central to the method.
For the real dataset, quantitative evaluation is limited to middle timesteps because ground truth is unavailable for non-middle timesteps, leaving temporal deblurring quality on real data unverified.

strengths: Addresses a novel and practically important problem: reconstructing sharp animatable 3D human Gaussian avatars directly from blurry videos, with a 3D-aware blur formation model integrated into 3DGS/SMPL.

Introduces a joint optimization framework combining B-spline sub-frame pose interpolation, a displacement CNN for high-frequency motion, inter-frame motion regularization, and refinement of shape/LBS weights, enabling recovery from coarse initialization.

Provides two new benchmarks: a synthetic blur dataset derived from ZJU-MoCap and a real 360-degree hybrid-exposure dataset with synchronized blurry/sharp cameras, supporting quantitative evaluation where none existed.

Extensive experiments and ablations demonstrate consistent improvements over 2D deblurring + GauHuman baselines on both synthetic and real data, and evaluate robustness to SMPL initialization noise, blur magnitude, view count, mask quality, novel poses, and smartphone capture.
Paper is generally clear, with detailed implementation settings and a plan to release code/datasets, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The blur formation model approximates real blur as an average of rendered sRGB images, ignoring nonlinear ISP/radiance-space integration and camera-induced blur; the authors acknowledge this, but it weakens the 'physics-based' claim and may limit synthetic benchmark fidelity.
The motion model is restricted to SMPL body joints, so it cannot recover motion of hands, face, clothing, or held objects; this limits generality in real-world avatars.

The real-world benchmark is relatively small (4 blurry cameras, 8 sharp cameras/scenes), and the synthetic blur relies on RIFE interpolation plus frame averaging, which may not fully match real motion blur distributions.

Several ablations show only modest gains (e.g., shape optimization, LBS refinement, control-knot count), and the inter-frame regularization slightly degrades the middle timestep in one setting, so the benefit of some components is not uniformly large.

Comparisons are limited to 2D deblurring methods combined with GauHuman; no comparison to 3D-aware dynamic deblurring Gaussian Splatting methods (e.g., BARD-GS) is provided, although adapting them to animatable avatars may not be straightforward.
Only image-space metrics are reported; geometry/shape accuracy of the reconstructed avatars is not quantitatively evaluated, despite the task being 3D reconstruction.
Notation is sometimes inconsistent (e.g., T used for exposure time/virtual frame number), and some equations could be clearer.

strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable 3D human avatars directly from blurry multi-view videos.

Proposes a 3D-aware blur formation model that connects SMPL-based human motion with 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering, enabling joint optimization of motion parameters and canonical avatar representation.
Introduces a motion model with B-spline sub-frame pose interpolation, learned pose displacement, inter-frame geodesic regularization, and LBS/shape refinement to mitigate motion ambiguity.

Constructs both a synthetic benchmark based on ZJU-MoCap and a real hybrid-exposure 360-degree camera dataset, with extensive ablations on blur magnitude, view number, masks, SMPL initialization, trajectory representation, and virtual sharp image number.

Reports consistent improvements over direct and two-stage 2D deblurring + GauHuman baselines on synthetic and real datasets in PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, and includes qualitative comparisons, novel-pose animation, and a smartphone demo.
weaknesses: The central motion-aware claim is not directly validated: no quantitative motion metrics (e.g., MPJPE, shape error, temporal consistency) are reported, despite optimizing SMPL pose/shape/LBS. Evaluation relies on rendering PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, so it is unclear whether motion is recovered correctly or the model mainly overfits the blur formation.

Baseline comparisons omit recent 3D-aware deblurring methods (e.g., BARD-GS, Deblur-NeRF, DP-NeRF, Bad-Gaussians, Dyblur) and other avatar models (e.g., 3DGS-Avatar, GaussianAvatar). Only 2D deblurring + GauHuman and direct GauHuman are compared, so claims of superiority over existing 3D deblurring/avatar approaches are not fully established.

The synthetic blur is generated by averaging sRGB frames after RIFE interpolation, which is not physically faithful: real blur integrates linear radiance before ISP/tone mapping. The authors acknowledge this limitation but still train/evaluate on sRGB-domain averaging, potentially biasing results in favor of the proposed model.

The real-world dataset is small (8 scenes, 4 blurry views, 8 sharp views) and lacks ground-truth SMPL/motion for quantitative motion evaluation. No error bars or statistical significance tests are provided, making marginal differences hard to interpret.

Several proposed components show marginal or inconsistent gains: e.g., Table 3 shape optimization 25.529 vs. 25.546, LBS 25.394 vs. 25.546; Table 5 B-spline 25.546 vs. linear 25.516; Table 6 differences under 0.03 dB; Table 12 mask differences under 0.12 dB; Table 14 with N_view=2, ours 23.331 vs. w/o shape 23.411. This weakens the claim that all components are necessary.

Reproducibility is limited: key details are missing, including canonical 3DGS initialization, architectures/hyperparameters of G_disp and the δ CNN, loss weight λ in Eq. 11, per-Gaussian LBS weight mapping, and how B-spline interpolation is applied to SO(3) rotations.

Mathematical/notation issues reduce clarity: Eq. 6's binomial factor appears miswritten (C_{P-1-i}^{P-1} evaluates to zero for i>0), Eq. 11 omits the regularization weight, R^{3×H×W} notation is nonstandard, and the 'physics-based' label is overstated given sRGB averaging. The title also contains a typo ('Animateable').
No runtime/computational cost analysis is provided, and no perceptual/user study or temporal flicker metrics are reported for a deblurring task where temporal coherence is important.
